title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
text:
Bottom line. Bender’s most-used word is his own name (206 times), then “fry” (158). “Ass” is only his 7th most-used word, but he says it 67 times, more than anyone else in the show.
In “War Is the H-Word,” the plot turns on a bomb that will go off when Bender says his most-used word. Fans have always assumed they know what that word is. I counted every word Bender says across all 140 episodes to check.

title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
section: His top word is his own name
text:
His top word is his own name
Bender talks about Bender a lot. After removing common words like “the” and “I,” and filler like “hey” and “yeah,” his own name tops the list, followed by his best friend’s.


Show code
plot_top <- function(mode) {
  top_words |>
    filter(rank <= 15) |>
    slice_head(n = 15) |>
    mutate(word = fct_reorder(word, n), is_ass = word == "ass") |>
    ggplot(aes(n, word, fill = is_ass)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.72) +
    geom_text(aes(label = n, fontface = ifelse(is_ass, "bold", "plain")),
              hjust = -0.25, size = 3.6, colour = label_ink(mode)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pe_green, `TRUE` = focus)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
    labs(x = "Times said", y = NULL) +
    theme_pe(mode)
}
plot_top("light")
plot_top("dark")




Bender’s 15 most-used words







Bender’s 15 most-used words





Ties share a rank, so “god” and “guys” are both 9th. Stemming, which folds “asses” into “ass” but also merges other words’ variants, drops “ass” to 10th.

title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
text:
Nobody says “ass” more
He may not say it most often, but he says it more than anyone else, and it isn’t close. Fry is a distant second with 14.


Show code
plot_ass <- function(mode) {
  ass_users |>
    slice_max(ass_exact, n = 8, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    mutate(speaker = fct_reorder(speaker, ass_exact), is_bender = speaker == "Bender") |>
    ggplot(aes(ass_exact, speaker, fill = is_bender)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.72) +
    geom_text(aes(label = ass_exact), hjust = -0.3, size = 3.6, colour = label_ink(mode)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pe_green, `TRUE` = focus)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
    labs(x = "Times said \"ass\"", y = NULL) +
    theme_pe(mode)
}
plot_ass("light")
plot_ass("dark")

title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
text:
Per word spoken, it’s closer
Bender also talks more than almost anyone, so raw counts flatter him. Scaling by how much each character says changes the picture: among characters with at least 2,000 words, Mom says “ass” at a slightly higher rate. That rests on just 5 uses, though, so I wouldn’t put much weight on it.


Show code
rate_data <- totals |>
  filter(words >= 2000) |>
  left_join(select(ass_users, speaker, ass_exact), by = "speaker") |>
  filter(coalesce(ass_exact, 0) > 0) |>   # characters who say it at least once
  mutate(
         rate = 1e4 * ass_exact / words,
         speaker = fct_reorder(speaker, rate),
         is_bender = speaker == "Bender")

plot_rate <- function(mode) {
  ggplot(rate_data, aes(rate, speaker, colour = is_bender)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = rate, yend = speaker), linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_point(size = 3.2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0(ass_exact, ifelse(ass_exact == 1, " use", " uses"))), hjust = -0.25, size = 3.3,
              colour = if (mode == "light") "#5f6670" else "#aab1ba") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pe_green, `TRUE` = focus)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
    labs(x = "Per 10,000 words spoken", y = NULL) +
    theme_pe(mode)
}
plot_rate("light")
plot_rate("dark")

title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
text:
How this was done






NoteMethods and limitations





Data. Transcripts of all 140 broadcast episodes from The Infosphere, collected in 2023. The 140 include the four films, which aired as 16 “Part” episodes. Only aggregated counts are published here; the transcripts and scraping code are not.
Cleaning. Most transcript pages had never been split into speaker and line, so I re-split every line on its first colon. That kept 1,010 lines that contain a second colon, which my 2023 version cut off. Stage directions in brackets and parentheses are removed from both the speaker and the line. Alternate-universe, robot, and ghost versions of the main cast count as the same character. The result is 28,949 spoken lines.
Words. Tokenized with tidytext. Common words are removed using tidytext’s stop-word lists, plus interjections and filler (“hey,” “yeah,” “uh,” “gonna,” and stretched spellings like “ohhhh”). Stemming uses the Porter stemmer. Ties share a rank.
Why remove filler. With stop words alone, “hey” edges out “bender” as his top word:









Definition
Top five




Stop words and filler removed (used here)
bender (206), fry (158), robot (123), time (84), wait (83)


Stop words only
hey (212), bender (206), yeah (172), fry (158), robot (123)





What changed from 2023. The original version of this analysis (published on LinkedIn) counted “bender” 375 times. That was inflated: its cleaning removed parenthetical directions but left bracketed ones like “[Bender walks in]” in the dialogue.
Limitations. Two episodes are mostly missing from the source: “Naturama” is one unsplit block of text and “Saturday Morning Fun Pit” largely is too, so those blocks are left out. “Zapp Dingbat” and “Meanwhile” have short transcripts at the source. Fan transcripts also miss or mishear some lines.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
text: Bottom line. Adopting an MCO model does appear to reduce annual per-enrollee expenditures to IDD waiver services.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: Why states moved I/DD services into managed care
text:
Why states moved I/DD services into managed care

States moved I/DD services from fee-for-service into managed care for largely the same reasons they’ve moved other Medicaid programs: more predictable budgets and slower cost growth. Under fee-for-service, the state pays providers for each service delivered, so spending rises with use. Most managed care arrangements instead pay a plan a fixed monthly amount per enrollee, called a capitation rate, and the plan takes on the financial risk of covering everyone’s services within it. That should give the state a predictable cost per person and gives the plan a reason to manage care efficiently, through care coordination, shifting services from institutions to community settings, negotiating provider rates. Critics worry the savings can also come from people getting less: plans may approve fewer services, pay less for what they approve, or leave providers with rates so low they deliver fewer hours than authorized.


Show code
adopt |>
  transmute(State = state, Program = program, `Year adopted` = adoption_year) |>
  knitr::kable()

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: What the spending data shows before any model
text:
What the spending data shows before any model

Adopting states started all over the map, but most ended up spending less per enrollee than they had before, even as typical states kept spending more.
Before adoption, these seven states don’t look alike. Arizona and Michigan spent well below the typical range, North Carolina tracked the median, and Kansas and Iowa spent far above it. What they share is what happens next. In Michigan, Wisconsin, North Carolina and Iowa, spending per enrollee in the I/DD category drops around the adoption year and stays down while the grey band keeps climbing, so the gap widens over time. Michigan falls by roughly half right after 1998 and stays flat for two decades.
The timing presents some challenges. In North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa, spending starts falling several years before the adoption year marked here. That could be states preparing for the switch, for example by restructuring waivers or tightening rates ahead of it, or it could mean the coded year is late. It also matters that Kansas, Iowa and North Carolina were spending well above typical states at their peaks, and unusually high spending tends to drift back toward the middle on its own. Those early declines are why the event study below checks for pre-existing trends.

All adoptersExplore a state








Figure 2: Medicaid spending per enrollee in the I/DD category. Grey band: middle half of states that never adopted. Dashed line: adoption year.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: Spending fell after adoption, and kept falling
text:
Spending fell after adoption, and kept falling

Spending per enrollee in the I/DD category fell as soon as states adopted managed care, kept falling for about a decade, and never recovered.
Compared with states that never adopted, adopters’ spending dropped by about $324 in the adoption year and kept falling, to about $1,033 below never-adopters ten or more years later. Averaged over all post-adoption years, the drop is $728 per enrollee. Two cautions: past about seven years, the estimates rest on Michigan and Wisconsin alone, and adopters’ spending was already drifting down relative to other states in the years before adoption. “How much should you trust this?” tests whether that earlier drift could explain the drop.






Figure 3: Change in I/DD-category spending per enrollee relative to the year before adoption, with 95% confidence intervals









NoteWhy not a simple before-and-after comparison?

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: The drop is spending, not more enrollees
text:
The drop is spending, not more enrollees

The per-enrollee expenditures are not better explained by changes in enrollment which remained fairly steady in adopting states.






Figure 4: Log I/DD-category spending and log Medicaid enrollment around adoption

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: The money didn’t move to other Medicaid services
text:
The money didn’t move to other Medicaid services

Cutting spending in one part of Medicaid can push costs somewhere else, either because services get recorded under a different category or because cuts in one service raise demand for others, such as fewer home supports leading to more hospital or nursing home care. If that were happening, other categories would rise to offset the I/DD drop. They don’t. The categories that rose add up to about $192, none of them by a clearly measurable amount, and prescription drugs actually fell slightly. Total spending per enrollee on personal health care fell by $632, about 87% of the $724 drop in the I/DD category. Nearly all of the change comes from that category.
One shift this can’t rule out: these categories cover spending on services only. Any part of a capitated payment that a plan keeps for administration or margin falls outside them entirely.






Figure 5: Effect of adoption on Medicaid spending per enrollee, by service category

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: How much should you trust this?
text:
How much should you trust this?

Adopters’ spending was already drifting down before adoption: in this window it falls from about $197 above its pre-adoption level seven years out to zero, roughly $33 a year. That could reflect states preparing for the switch, such as restructuring waivers or holding down rates beforehand, or high spenders drifting back toward the middle. But the drift can’t account for what happens at adoption. Holding the comparison to the same five states throughout (Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, North Carolina and Wisconsin), spending drops $312 in the first year alone, about ten times the yearly drift. By year three it is $549 below its pre-adoption level, where the earlier drift alone would have predicted about $131. Averaged over the four post-adoption years, the drop is $443.

Same states, same window







Figure 6: Event study restricted to a balanced window





Could this happen by chance?

With only six adopting states, the usual standard errors aren’t reliable, so I checked the result another way: assign the same adoption years to randomly chosen states and see how big an “effect” shows up by chance. I did this 1000 times. None of the random assignments produced a drop as large as the real one (p < 0.001). That makes chance an unlikely explanation, though on its own it can’t rule out adopters differing from other states in some other way.






Figure 7: The actual estimate against 1,000 placebo adoption assignments









NoteWhy randomization inference?






Standard errors clustered by state assume there are many independent groups to learn from. Here only six states ever change treatment status, so clustered standard errors tend to be too small and confidence intervals too narrow. Randomization inference sidesteps that problem.
The procedure: take the six real adoption years, shuffle them, and assign them to six states drawn at random from the 50 states and DC (Arizona excluded, since it adopted before the data begin). Re-estimate the two-way fixed effects model on this fake assignment and record the estimate. Repeating this 1000 times builds the distribution of estimates you’d see if adoption had no effect anywhere. The p-value is the share of placebo estimates at least as large in absolute value as the real one.
Two limits. First, it assumes any state could plausibly have been an adopter; if adopters were systematically different, the comparison is less clean. Second, it tests the simpler two-way fixed effects estimate rather than the Sun–Abraham event study, and it doesn’t address the pre-adoption drift. That’s what the balanced-window check is for.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
text:
What this can’t tell us

This analysis shows that spending fell. It can’t show whether quality of care changed with it. The limited evidence on experience is mixed: people with I/DD in Illinois managed care described problems with access and navigating the system (Gibbons, Owen, & Heller, 2016), and some family caregivers in four managed-care states reported less flexibility and harder access to services (Williamson et al., 2016). Nor can this data separate lower prices from fewer services: spending can fall because care costs less or because less of it is delivered.
The data also misses money that never reaches services. CMS’s personal health care figures exclude administrative costs, including what managed care plans keep for administration and margin. Before drawing policy conclusions, a state would want to confirm that those costs are small enough not to cancel out the savings in service spending.
